Generative AI retrieval product for an enterprise client

In production
Capisoft · 2026 · project manager, product owner and consultant on the same engagement · client acquisition through to delivery

A maritime enterprise was running five disconnected business systems, which meant nobody could answer a straightforward operational question without asking three people. I found this client through direct outreach, ran the discovery sessions that scoped the problem, then built the solution: one cloud knowledge base across Azure and AWS, with schema conflicts resolved so the same entity resolved consistently everywhere, and a retrieval layer that answers questions from company data in plain language.

Success criteria were agreed before the build, not after: answers grounded in source data, and fast enough to use mid-conversation. A domain expert and the development team validated the result together. I wrote the technical work personally in Python, SQL and Cypher, and presented the outcome to senior decision-makers in a twelve-slide executive format.

Access governance for hospital medication logistics

MSc thesis
HagaHospital, The Hague · eight months on site · graduated July 2026

Autonomous delivery robots were going to move medication from pharmacy to ward. The open question was who should be allowed to open which compartment, and when. I spent eight months inside the hospital interviewing and observing staff across nine distinct roles and built an access model where permission depends not only on who you are but on what state the robot is in, so a nurse can reach a delivery at the ward but not during transit.

Every requirement traces back to a named stakeholder group rather than an assumption. I quantified risk with an FMEA, setting the intervention threshold before scoring anything, and when the highest score came in under that threshold I reported exactly that instead of adjusting the number to produce a finding. The whole design was validated line by line against GDPR, NEN 7510, ISO 14971 and the Opiumwet, with a tamper-evident audit log so every access event stays verifiable afterwards.

I then built a 23-scenario browser simulator and used it to walk the same clinicians through the system and collect their reactions, which is where several of the final design decisions actually came from.

Self-driving robot, full deep learning lifecycle

Deployed
Applied Data Science · PyTorch · December 2025

End to end, from empty folder to a robot driving itself. I collected and labelled roughly 4,000 images, designed a five-layer convolutional network, and ran controlled experiments rather than guessing: five network depths compared under identical conditions, four learning rates swept, final model selected on out-of-sample evidence.

One experiment failed. Heavy data augmentation, which should in theory have helped, made the error substantially worse. I reported it in full rather than dropping it from the write-up. The final model went onto a Raspberry Pi running inference every few milliseconds, and I tested it across five physical tracks plus deliberately adversarial conditions until the remaining failures traced to hardware rather than to the model.

Gezelschap, a care-matching platform

Won, specified and built
Capisoft · client acquisition, requirements and build, by one person

This project is the entire job in one piece of work. I landed the client, took their requirements, and built the product. Most organisations split that across three people and two departments: someone who wins the work, someone who specifies it, someone who builds it. Here it was one person from first conversation to running software, and nothing was lost in the handovers because there were none.

The client needed to match people who need companionship care with the right carer. I ran the requirements sessions to find out what that actually meant in practice, which is where the real problem surfaced: matching is the easy half. Trust is the hard half, because you are sending a stranger into a vulnerable person's home. So the system I built is as much an identity and screening chain as a matching engine, with identity verification, background screening, document checks and liveness detection sitting in front of the matching and recommendation logic, plus reminder and alert flows around the visits themselves.

Then I built the console the operators run the service from, pictured below: queues for KYC checks, certificates and contracts, user and lead management, and a metrics layer covering match rate, completion rate, repeat requests and hours logged. Measurement was designed in from the start rather than bolted on once someone asked for a report.

Real estate investment advisory and financial modelling

Client work
Xtra Real Estate, 2022 - 2024 · Nexus Real Estate and Asset Management, founder, 2024

Before the AI work, I ran money. I advised 8 clients on a €2M income-producing real estate portfolio, and the recommendation was never the starting point, the model was. For each asset I built the quantitative case: asset-level yield, rental cash flow performance, financing cost coverage and downside risk, then assessed repayment capacity and the regulatory constraints attached to each transaction. The portfolio returned 23% average ROI over 18 months.

The habit that transferred most directly into my technical work came from what happened after the deal. I monitored realised performance against modelled expectations to catch drift early, found the underperforming assets before they became losses, and adjusted exposure on quantitative evidence rather than on instinct or hope. That is the same discipline as watching a model in production and acting when its real-world behaviour separates from what the validation set promised.

I also had to make all of it understood. My clients were an international group across very different levels of seniority and background, and explaining a financing-cost-coverage calculation to someone who is about to commit real money, in language they can actually interrogate, is a harder communication problem than any technical presentation I have given since. In 2024 I founded Nexus Real Estate and Asset Management in Tirana, generated the leads, built the client base and ran the commercials myself, then liquidated my stake cleanly on relocating to the Netherlands rather than leaving it dormant.

Comparative graph analytics study

Research
Neo4j and HyperNetX · tooling recommendation

Two competing data models built on the same fragmented dataset, cleaned first, then compared head to head using shortest-path and breadth-first analysis. Average traversal dropped from three or four steps to 2.14. The deliverable was not the model, it was the recommendation: network visualisations and a quantitative comparison table that let the decision-makers choose a tool on evidence.

PRISM, a multi-agent AI system

In development
Personal project · unfinished, no track record claimed

Something I build in my own time to stay close to the technology. A modular data layer, an AI decision engine, a deterministic rule validator that can veto the model, and an audit database recording every decision against its outcome. A nightly loop has the agents analyse their own failed decisions and propose changes for human review. I built it that way because I wanted performance measured on record rather than on recollection. It is not finished, and I would not claim results from it.

How I work

I translate business requirements into AI solutions, in that order. The requirement comes first and the technology second, which sounds obvious and almost never happens. In the hospital that meant turning interviews with nine clinical roles into a 31-item specification before a line of the system was designed. At the consultancy it meant running discovery with the client to find where the problem was actually expensive, then scoping the AI solution against that, rather than arriving with a product and hunting for somewhere to put it.

I agree what success means before building. On the retrieval product the accuracy and response-time targets were set with the client up front, which is why there was something to validate against at the end rather than a debate about whether it was good enough.

I report the result I got, not the one I wanted. The augmentation experiment that made the model worse is in the report. So is the risk threshold that was never crossed. In work people make decisions on, an analyst who tells you when the data does not support the conclusion is worth more than one who always finds something.

I go and ask the people who do the job. Nine roles in a hospital, a domain expert on the client side, eight private investment clients before that. Most problems that look technical turn out, on inspection, to be process and information problems.
